title: Working in Canada: What Express Entry Really Involves
excerpt: Express Entry is a points system with published rules, real cutoffs and real costs. Here is an honest walk through the CRS, category draws, provincial nominations and what to budget before you start.
content:
A friend of mine in Lagos spent two years telling everyone he was "processing Canada." When I finally asked what stage he had reached, the truth came out. No language test, no idea what his score was, and a consultant charging him monthly to "monitor draws" that anyone can check online for free. If that story stings a little, this guide is for you. Express Entry is not a lottery and it is not a mystery. It is a ranking system with published rules, published cutoffs and published fees, all sitting on Canada.ca for anyone patient enough to read them. Let's walk through it the way I wish someone had walked him through it.

Express Entry manages three federal programs: the Federal Skilled Worker Program, which covers most first-time applicants from Africa, the Canadian Experience Class for people who have already worked in Canada, and the Federal Skilled Trades Program. You create a profile, the system scores you, and the highest-ranked candidates get invited to apply for permanent residence.

The process, step by step

  1. Take an approved language test. The approved English tests are IELTS General Training, CELPIP-General and PTE Core; French speakers take TEF Canada or TCF Canada. Language is the biggest points lever you fully control, so treat the test like a professional exam, not a formality. A candidate in Accra who moves from a good band to a great one can gain more points than a second degree would give her.
  2. Get your credentials assessed. If you studied outside Canada, you need an Educational Credential Assessment, which confirms that your degree from Ibadan, Legon or Wits equals a Canadian credential. Budget several weeks for it.
  3. Calculate your score honestly. Use the official calculator before you spend serious money. If the number is low, the honest fixes are better language scores, French, or a provincial route, not a consultant's promises.
  4. Create your profile and enter the pool. Creating a profile costs nothing. You sit in the pool, ranked against every other candidate.
  5. Wait for a draw that fits you. Invitations go out in rounds through the year: general rounds, program-specific rounds such as Provincial Nominee Program draws, and category rounds for particular occupations and for French speakers.
  6. If invited, apply within 60 days. An Invitation to Apply comes with a hard 60 day deadline, so gather your documents before you are invited, not after. You will upload everything, pay your fees, give biometrics and take a medical exam with an approved panel physician.
  7. Wait for a decision. Processing time varies by program. As one reference point, Canada.ca currently lists about 7 months for provincial nominee applications that come through Express Entry.

How the points actually stack up

The Comprehensive Ranking System is the heart of the whole thing. Every candidate gets a score, every draw has a cutoff, and the maths is public. The table below shows the major factors for a single applicant, drawn from the official CRS criteria.

CRS factorMaximum points (single applicant)
Official language proficiency160
Level of education150
Age110
Canadian work experience80
Skill transferability combinations100
Provincial or territorial nomination600
French language skills50
Post-secondary study in Canada30
Sibling living in Canada15

Notice what is missing: a job offer. Since March 25, 2025, job offers earn zero CRS points. If anyone offers to sell you a "Canadian job offer" to raise your score, they are selling something the system no longer counts. Walk away.

Category draws: why your occupation suddenly matters

Alongside general rounds, IRCC runs category-based selection: draws restricted to people with experience in fields Canada needs. The current categories cover healthcare and social services, STEM, trades, education, transport and French-language proficiency, plus newer streams for physicians, researchers and senior managers with Canadian experience, and skilled military recruits. Category draws matter because their cutoffs sit well below general ones. In the published draw history, a healthcare round on June 25, 2026 invited 4,000 people with a cutoff of 475, and a French-language round on May 28, 2026 invited 4,500 at just 409, while a Canadian Experience Class round on June 23, 2026 cut off at 516. Strong French has been worth roughly a hundred points of forgiveness, and it stacks with the 50 bonus points in the table above. Serious French study is the most underrated move available to you.

The 600 point lifeline: provincial nomination

Eleven provinces and territories run Provincial Nominee Programs; Quebec and Nunavut sit outside the system. Each province picks candidates whose skills match its own labour needs, and a nomination adds 600 points to your score, which all but guarantees an invitation. That is why PNP draw cutoffs look terrifying at first glance, like the 730 cutoff in the June 22, 2026 round: everyone in that draw already carried the 600 point bonus. The practical lesson is to research which provinces actively want your occupation, because a nurse from Nairobi and a software developer from Johannesburg may find their fastest doors in completely different provinces.

What it really costs

Here is the part consultants tend to blur. The government fees are fixed and public: 1,590 Canadian dollars per adult including the right of permanent residence fee, and 270 dollars per dependent child, plus 85 dollars for biometrics. Before any of that, you will pay for your language test, your credential assessment, medicals and police certificates. Then there is proof of funds: currently 15,263 Canadian dollars for a single applicant, 19,001 for a couple and 28,362 for a family of four. This must be your own accessible money, shown through bank letters, not a loan from an uncle that goes back the week after. The comfort is in the sequencing: the big fees only land after you are invited, so the early spending is limited to tests and assessments.

Documents to gather early

  • A valid passport for you and every family member
  • Language test results that will still be valid when you apply
  • Your Educational Credential Assessment report
  • Police certificates from countries where you have lived
  • Bank letters showing your settlement funds, including six month average balances
  • Birth, marriage or divorce certificates where they apply
  • Medical exam results from an approved panel physician

A realistic expectations check

Now the paragraph I ask you to read twice. A single applicant abroad with strong English, a master's degree and no Canadian connections often scores in the mid 400s. That clears some category draws. It does not clear Canadian Experience Class rounds, which have stayed above 500, and the published history shows no general round open to all programs since April 2024, so the realistic doors for a candidate abroad are category draws, French and provincial nomination. That is not a reason to quit; it is a reason to plan properly. Expect the full journey, from booking your first test to holding a visa, to take a year or two. Expect to spend money with no guaranteed outcome. Do not resign from your job on the strength of a pool profile, and be wary of anyone who promises certainty for a fee. The people I have watched succeed treated Canada as one option in a wider strategy: they compared it against routes like the one in our practical guide to working in the UK, kept their income growing at home, some by earning globally while living locally, and kept improving the fundamentals that pay off in any country. Because here is the quiet truth about landing in Toronto or Calgary: permanent residence gets you in the door, but you will still need a CV that gets you interviews and the persistence to rebuild your professional network from scratch.

My Lagos friend, by the way, finally took his IELTS, discovered his score, and made a two year plan around French classes and a province that wanted his skills. He stopped "processing Canada" and started preparing for it. That is the whole difference, and it is available to you today.
